input.question: Which educational institution did Petia R. Parpoulova attend?

documents.text: As Petia R. Parpoulova sat in her office, surrounded by stacks of dusty tomes and scattered notes, she couldn't help but think back to the formative years that had shaped her into the scholar she was today. The warm, golden light of the Mexican sun still lingered in her memory, a reminder of the time she spent at the National Autonomous University of Mexico. It was there, amidst the vibrant streets of Mexico City, that Petia had discovered her passion for comparative literature. She recalled the lively debates in Professor Ortega's seminar, where the works of Octavio Paz and Jorge Luis Borges were dissected with the same fervor as the latest soccer match. The university's sprawling campus, with its mix of colonial and modern architecture, had been her playground, where she would often get lost in the labyrinthine corridors, stumbling upon hidden courtyards and secret gardens. One particular afternoon, while researching in the university's library, Petia had stumbled upon an obscure text by a 19th-century Mexican writer, which would later become the foundation of her dissertation. The musty smell of the old book still lingered in her nostrils, transporting her back to that moment of discovery. As she delved deeper into her research, Petia's fascination with the intersection of cultures and literatures only grew stronger. Her time at the National Autonomous University of Mexico had instilled in her a sense of curiosity and adventure, which she carried with her to the University of Washington, where she would eventually earn her Ph.D. in Comparative Literature. The memories of those formative years still whispered in her ear, guiding her as she navigated the complex landscape of literary theory and criticism.
